items.title: 14.2.5 Dot Product of Vectors in terms of their components

blocks.text: Let \(\underline{u} = a_{1}\underline{i} + b_{1}\underline{i} + c_{1}\underline{k}\) and \(\underline{v} = a_{2}\underline{i} + b_{2}\underline{i} + c_{2}\underline{k}\) be two non-zero vectors.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
The book prints \(b_{1}\underline{i}\) and \(b_{2}\underline{i}\) as the middle terms. They should be \(b_{1}\underline{j}\) and \(b_{2}\underline{j}\):
\[\underline{u} = a_{1}\underline{i} + b_{1}\underline{j} + c_{1}\underline{k}\]
\[\underline{v} = a_{2}\underline{i} + b_{2}\underline{j} + c_{2}\underline{k}\]
The working that follows uses \(\underline{j}\), as it should.

From distributive law we can write:
\[\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = (a_{1}\underline{i} + b_{1}\underline{j} + c_{1}\underline{k})\]
\[\cdot\ (a_{2}\underline{i} + b_{2}\underline{j} + c_{2}\underline{k})\]
\[= a_{1}a_{2}(\underline{i} \cdot \underline{i}) + a_{1}b_{2}(\underline{i} \cdot \underline{j})\]
\[+ a_{1}c_{2}(\underline{i} \cdot \underline{k}) + b_{1}a_{2}(\underline{j} \cdot \underline{i})\]
\[+ b_{1}b_{2}(\underline{j} \cdot \underline{j}) + b_{1}c_{2}(\underline{j} \cdot \underline{k})\]
\[+ c_{1}a_{2}(\underline{k} \cdot \underline{i}) + c_{1}b_{2}(\underline{k} \cdot \underline{j})\]
\[+ c_{1}c_{2}(\underline{k} \cdot \underline{k})\]

\[\Rightarrow \underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = a_{1}a_{2} + b_{1}b_{2} + c_{1}c_{2}\]
because
\[\underline{i} \cdot \underline{i} = \underline{j} \cdot \underline{j} = \underline{k} \cdot \underline{k} = 1\]
\[\underline{i} \cdot \underline{j} = \underline{j} \cdot \underline{k} = \underline{k} \cdot \underline{i} = 0\]
Hence the dot product of two vectors is the sum of the product of their corresponding components.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Expanding the brackets gives \(3 \times 3 = 9\) terms. By 14.2.2, the six terms with two different unit vectors are \(0\) and the three terms with the same unit vector twice keep their coefficient. That is why only \(a_{1}a_{2}\), \(b_{1}b_{2}\), \(c_{1}c_{2}\) remain.
Quick example of ours: \((2\underline{i} - \underline{j} + 3\underline{k}) \cdot (\underline{i} + 4\underline{j} + 2\underline{k}) = 2 - 4 + 6 = 4\).

blocks.title: Example 6
blocks.problem: Show that the components of a vector are the projections of that vector along \(\underline{i}\), \(\underline{j}\) and \(\underline{k}\) respectively.
steps:
Given: a vector \(\underline{v} = a\underline{i} + b\underline{j} + c\underline{k}\).
To prove: its projections along \(\underline{i}\), \(\underline{j}\), \(\underline{k}\) are \(a\), \(b\), \(c\).
Method: use the projection formula of 14.2.3: projection of \(\underline{v}\) along \(\underline{u}\) is \(\frac{\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v}}{|\underline{u}|}\), here with \(\underline{u} = \underline{i}, \underline{j}, \underline{k}\), whose magnitudes are \(1\).

Step 1: Projection along \(\underline{i}\)
\[\dfrac{\underline{v} \cdot \underline{i}}{|\underline{i}|} = (a\underline{i} + b\underline{j} + c\underline{k}) \cdot \underline{i}\]
\[= a(1) + b(0) + c(0) = a\]
Why: \(|\underline{i}| = 1\), and by 14.2.2, \(\underline{i} \cdot \underline{i} = 1\), \(\underline{j} \cdot \underline{i} = 0\), \(\underline{k} \cdot \underline{i} = 0\).

Step 2: Projection along \(\underline{j}\)
\[\dfrac{\underline{v} \cdot \underline{j}}{|\underline{j}|} = (a\underline{i} + b\underline{j} + c\underline{k}) \cdot \underline{j} = b\]
Why: only \(\underline{j} \cdot \underline{j} = 1\) survives; the other two products are \(0\).

Step 3: Projection along \(\underline{k}\)
\[\dfrac{\underline{v} \cdot \underline{k}}{|\underline{k}|} = (a\underline{i} + b\underline{j} + c\underline{k}) \cdot \underline{k} = c\]
Why: only \(\underline{k} \cdot \underline{k} = 1\) survives.

Check:
Take \(\underline{v} = 2\underline{i} - 3\underline{j} + 5\underline{k}\): \(\underline{v} \cdot \underline{i} = 2\), \(\underline{v} \cdot \underline{j} = -3\), \(\underline{v} \cdot \underline{k} = 5\), exactly its components.
blocks.answer: Hence the components \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) of \(\underline{v} = a\underline{i} + b\underline{j} + c\underline{k}\) are the projections of \(\underline{v}\) along \(\underline{i}\), \(\underline{j}\) and \(\underline{k}\) respectively.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Example 6 shows the meaning of the components: \(a\) is how far \(\underline{v}\) reaches along the \(x\)-axis, \(b\) along the \(y\)-axis and \(c\) along the \(z\)-axis.

blocks.title: Example 7
blocks.problem:
Prove that in any triangle \(ABC\)
(i) \(a^{2} = b^{2} + c^{2} - 2bc\cos A\) (Cosine Law)
(ii) \(a = b\cos C + c\cos B\) (Projection Law)
steps:
Given: triangle \(ABC\) with side lengths \(a = BC\), \(b = CA\), \(c = AB\).
To prove: (i) the cosine law, (ii) the projection law.
Method: take vectors \(\underline{a}\), \(\underline{b}\), \(\underline{c}\) along \(BC\), \(CA\), \(AB\) (head to tail round the triangle, as in the figures). Then \(\underline{a} + \underline{b} + \underline{c} = \underline{0}\). Dot this equation with suitable vectors and use \(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = |\underline{u}||\underline{v}|\cos\theta\).

Step 1: The vectors close the triangle
\[\underline{a} + \underline{b} + \underline{c} = \underline{0}\]
Why: going from \(B\) to \(C\), then \(C\) to \(A\), then \(A\) to \(B\) brings us back to the start, so the total displacement is zero.

(i) Step 2: Make \(\underline{a}\) the subject
\[\underline{a} = -(\underline{b} + \underline{c})\]
Why: we want \(a^{2} = \underline{a} \cdot \underline{a}\) in terms of \(b\) and \(c\).

(i) Step 3: Dot each side with itself
\[\underline{a} \cdot \underline{a} = (\underline{b} + \underline{c}) \cdot (\underline{b} + \underline{c})\]
\[= \underline{b} \cdot \underline{b} + \underline{b} \cdot \underline{c} + \underline{c} \cdot \underline{b} + \underline{c} \cdot \underline{c}\]
Why: \((-1)(-1) = 1\), and the distributive property opens the brackets like algebra.

(i) Step 4: Use \(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{u} = |\underline{u}|^{2}\) and commutativity
\[a^{2} = b^{2} + 2\underline{b} \cdot \underline{c} + c^{2}\]
Why: \(\underline{b} \cdot \underline{c} = \underline{c} \cdot \underline{b}\), so the two middle terms add up.

(i) Step 5: The angle between \(\underline{b}\) and \(\underline{c}\)
\[\underline{b} \cdot \underline{c} = bc\cos(\pi - A)\]
\[a^{2} = b^{2} + c^{2} + 2bc\cos(\pi - A)\]
Why: \(\underline{b}\) points from \(C\) towards \(A\) and \(\underline{c}\) starts at \(A\). Placed tail to tail at \(A\), \(\underline{c}\) makes the exterior angle \(\pi - A\) with the extension of \(CA\) (first figure).

(i) Step 6: Use \(\cos(\pi - A) = -\cos A\)
\[a^{2} = b^{2} + c^{2} - 2bc\cos A\]
Why: this is the allied-angle identity: cosine is negative in the second quadrant.

(ii) Step 7: Write \(\underline{a}\) another way
\[\underline{a} = -\underline{b} - \underline{c}\]
Why: the same closing equation; now we dot with \(\underline{a}\) (not with itself on the right) to bring in \(\cos B\) and \(\cos C\).

(ii) Step 8: Take dot product with \(\underline{a}\)
\[\underline{a} \cdot \underline{a} = -\underline{a} \cdot \underline{b} - \underline{a} \cdot \underline{c}\]
Why: dotting both sides with the same vector keeps the equation true.

(ii) Step 9: Find the angles
\[= -ab\cos(\pi - C) - ac\cos(\pi - B)\]
Why: \(\underline{a}\) ends at \(C\) and \(\underline{b}\) starts at \(C\); tail to tail they make the exterior angle \(\pi - C\). Similarly \(\underline{c}\) ends at \(B\) and \(\underline{a}\) starts at \(B\), making \(\pi - B\) (second figure).

(ii) Step 10: Simplify the signs
\[= -ab(-\cos C) - ac(-\cos B)\]
\[a^{2} = ab\cos C + ac\cos B\]
Why: \(\cos(\pi - x) = -\cos x\), and two minus signs make a plus.

(ii) Step 11: Divide by \(a\)
\[a = b\cos C + c\cos B\]
Why: \(a\) is a side length, so \(a \ne 0\).

Check:
Right triangle with \(a = 5\), \(b = 4\), \(c = 3\) (right angle at \(A\)): \(\cos A = 0\), \(\cos B = \frac{3}{5}\), \(\cos C = \frac{4}{5}\).
\[b^{2} + c^{2} - 2bc\cos A = 16 + 9 - 0 = 25 = a^{2}\]
\[b\cos C + c\cos B = \tfrac{16}{5} + \tfrac{9}{5} = 5 = a\]
blocks.answer: (i) \(a^{2} = b^{2} + c^{2} - 2bc\cos A\) and (ii) \(a = b\cos C + c\cos B\), proved by the dot product.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The key idea in Example 7 is the angle between two vectors that follow each other round the triangle. The angle between two vectors is measured tail to tail. When one vector ends at a vertex and the next one starts there, we extend the first one beyond the vertex; the angle between them is then the exterior angle \(\pi - (\text{interior angle})\). That is where every \(\pi - A\), \(\pi - B\), \(\pi - C\) comes from.

blocks.title: Example 8
steps:
Given: angles \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) (take \(\alpha > \beta\)).
To prove: \(\cos(\alpha - \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta\).
Method: take two unit vectors at angles \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) with the \(x\)-axis and compute their dot product in two ways: by the angle and by components.

Step 1: The two unit vectors
Let \(\overrightarrow{OA}\) and \(\overrightarrow{OB}\) be unit vectors in the \(xy\)-plane making angles \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) with the positive \(x\)-axis, so that \(\angle AOB = \alpha - \beta\).
\[\overrightarrow{OA} = \cos\alpha\,\underline{i} + \sin\alpha\,\underline{j}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OB} = \cos\beta\,\underline{i} + \sin\beta\,\underline{j}\]
Why: a vector of length \(1\) at angle \(\alpha\) has \(x\)-component \(\cos\alpha\) and \(y\)-component \(\sin\alpha\) (definitions of cosine and sine).

Step 2: Dot product by components
\[\overrightarrow{OA} \cdot \overrightarrow{OB}\]
\[= (\cos\alpha\,\underline{i} + \sin\alpha\,\underline{j}) \cdot (\cos\beta\,\underline{i} + \sin\beta\,\underline{j})\]
\[= \cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta\]
Why: multiply matching components and add (14.2.5).

Step 3: Dot product by the angle
\[\overrightarrow{OA} \cdot \overrightarrow{OB} = |\overrightarrow{OA}||\overrightarrow{OB}|\cos(\alpha - \beta)\]
\[= \cos(\alpha - \beta)\]
Why: the angle between the vectors is \(\alpha - \beta\), and \(|\overrightarrow{OA}| = |\overrightarrow{OB}| = 1\).

Step 4: Equate
\[\cos(\alpha - \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta\]
Why: both expressions are the same dot product.

Check:
\(\alpha = 60^{\circ}\), \(\beta = 30^{\circ}\):
\[\cos 30^{\circ} = \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\]
\[\cos 60^{\circ}\cos 30^{\circ} + \sin 60^{\circ}\sin 30^{\circ} = \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4} + \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4} = \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\]

blocks.alt: Magenta x and y axes with origin O. Two cyan unit vectors OA and OB start at O; OA makes the larger angle alpha and OB the smaller angle beta with the positive x-axis. The angle between them is marked alpha minus beta.
blocks.caption: Figure: Example 8, unit vectors OA and OB with ∠AOB = α − β (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(\underline{u} \cdot \underline{v} = a_{1}a_{2} + b_{1}b_{2} + c_{1}c_{2}\): multiply matching components and add.
2. The components of a vector are its projections along \(\underline{i}\), \(\underline{j}\), \(\underline{k}\) (Example 6).
3. The dot product proves the cosine law, the projection law (Example 7) and \(\cos(\alpha - \beta)\) (Example 8).
4. For vectors following each other round a triangle, the angle between them is the exterior angle.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Multiplying non-matching components (\(a_{1}b_{2}\) etc.); those terms vanish because \(\underline{i} \cdot \underline{j} = 0\).
2. Using the interior angle \(A\) instead of \(\pi - A\) for vectors placed head to tail; this gives \(+2bc\cos A\), the wrong sign.
3. Forgetting that \(\cos(\pi - x) = -\cos x\).
